Orbit Lab
Unit 6 · Energy & Momentum of Rotating Systems
Start

AP Physics 1 · Unit 6 · Topics 6.1–6.6

Spinning things carry energy and momentum too.

Fidget spinners, figure skaters, bowling balls and satellites. Unit 6 takes the energy and momentum rules you learned in Units 3 and 4 and lets them spin.

About 50 minutes·9 hands-on labs·Arrow keys or the buttons below

The plan

Six stops. One big idea.

Units 3 and 4 gave you energy and momentum for things that slide. Unit 6 gives you the same two tools for things that spin.

6.1

Rotational Kinetic Energy

Spinning stores energy: \( K = \tfrac12 I\omega^2 \).

6.2

Torque and Work

A twist through an angle pushes energy in or pulls it out.

6.3

Angular Momentum & Impulse

How much spin something has, and what it takes to change it.

6.4

Conservation of Angular Momentum

No outside twist? The total spin can't change. Hello, figure skater.

6.5

Rolling

Sliding and spinning at once, locked together by \( v = r\omega \).

6.6

Orbiting Satellites

Energy and angular momentum steer moons, planets and satellites.

Big questions

Four puzzles this unit can solve.

  • 1
    Why does a skater spin faster when she pulls her arms in? Nobody pushed her. Something else is going on.
  • 2
    Why do planets speed up when they swing close to the Sun? It's the same rule as the skater.
  • 3
    What keeps a moving bicycle from tipping over? Its spinning wheels carry a lot of "spin" that fights being tilted.
  • 4
    What do satellites and thrown balls have in common? Both are falling. The satellite just moves sideways fast enough to keep missing the ground.

On the AP exam

Unit 6 is about 5–8% of the AP Physics 1 exam and takes roughly 8–14 class periods.

Expect "increase, decrease, or stay the same?" questions. The College Board says naming a law ("conservation of energy") is not enough. You have to explain each step.

Every idea here has a straight-line twin you already know. Look for the side-by-side twin cards.

The dictionary

Straight-line physics, translated into spin.

Straight line (Units 3–4)Spinning (Unit 6)
mass \( m \) (kg)how hard to speed up→rotational inertia \( I \) (kg·m²)how hard to spin up
velocity \( v \) (m/s)→angular velocity \( \omega \) (rad/s)
force \( F \) (N)→torque \( \tau \) (N·m)
kinetic energy \( \tfrac12 mv^2 \)→\( \tfrac12 I\omega^2 \)
work \( W = F\Delta x \)→\( W = \tau\Delta\theta \)
momentum \( p = mv \)→\( L = I\omega \)
impulse \( F\Delta t = \Delta p \)→\( \tau\Delta t = \Delta L \)
no outside force → \( p \) stays the same→no outside torque → \( L \) stays the same

How to read the symbols

\( \theta \) "theta": angle turned, in radians

\( \omega \) "omega": spin rate

\( \tau \) "tau": a twist (torque)

\( I \): rotational inertia, "spin laziness"

\( L \): angular momentum, "amount of spin"

The Unit 5 bridges still hold: \( v = r\omega \), \( \Delta x = r\Delta\theta \), \( a = r\alpha \).

Same shapes of equations. Swap \( m \to I \), \( v \to \omega \), \( F \to \tau \), \( x \to \theta \).

Topic 6.1 · the idea

A spinning thing has energy even if it goes nowhere.

Flick a fidget spinner. Its middle stays put between your fingers, yet it hums for a minute. Where is the energy hiding?

In the spin. Every little piece of the spinner travels around a circle, so every piece has a speed. Speed means kinetic energy. Add up all the pieces and you get rotational kinetic energy.

J joulesscalar no directionω in rad/s
Straight line · Unit 3

\[ K = \tfrac12 m v^2 \]

half × mass × speed²

⇅
Spinning · Unit 6

\[ K = \tfrac12 I\omega^2 \]

half × rotational inertia × spin rate²

\( I \) takes the place of mass, and \( \omega \) takes the place of speed. Same recipe, spinning ingredients.

Topic 6.1 · the equation

Two dials control spin energy.

I
Where the mass sits. Mass far from the axis moves fast and holds lots of energy. Mass near the axis barely moves. A hoop beats a solid disk of the same mass and size.
ω²
How fast it spins, squared. Double \( \omega \) and the energy becomes 4 times bigger. Triple it: 9 times.
Shape (mass \( M \), radius \( R \))\( I \)
Hoop (all mass on the rim)\( MR^2 \)
Hollow sphere\( \tfrac23 MR^2 \)
Solid disk or cylinder\( \tfrac12 MR^2 \)
Solid sphere\( \tfrac25 MR^2 \)

The AP exam gives you these when a problem needs them.

\[ K_{\text{rot}} = \tfrac12 I\omega^2 \]

half × spin laziness × spin rate²

Quick one

A wheel with \( I = 0.50\,\mathrm{kg{\cdot}m^2} \) spins at \( 4.0\,\mathrm{rad/s} \), then speeds up to \( 8.0\,\mathrm{rad/s} \).

\( K_1 = \tfrac12(0.50)(4.0)^2 = 4.0\,\mathrm{J} \)

\( K_2 = \tfrac12(0.50)(8.0)^2 = 16\,\mathrm{J} \)

Twice the spin, four times the energy.

Topic 6.1 · total kinetic energy

Moving and spinning at once? Add both energies.

Spins in place

A top, or a spinner on your finger. Its center of mass stays still.

\( K = \tfrac12 I\omega^2 \) only

Slides, no spin

A hockey puck gliding on ice. Every bit moves at the same speed.

\( K = \tfrac12 Mv^2 \) only

Rolls: both!

A bowling ball moves forward and spins at the same time.

\( K = \tfrac12 Mv^2 + \tfrac12 I\omega^2 \)

Straight-line part

\[ K_{\text{trans}} = \tfrac12 Mv_{\text{cm}}^2 \]

the center of mass moving through space

+
Spinning part

\[ K_{\text{rot}} = \tfrac12 I\omega^2 \]

spinning about the center of mass

Energy is a scalar: no arrows, no directions. Just add the two numbers to get \( K_{\text{tot}} \).

Worked examples

Three spin-energy problems, start to finish.

A · Spinning in place

A solid disk (\( M = 4.0\,\mathrm{kg} \), \( R = 0.30\,\mathrm{m} \)) spins at \( 10\,\mathrm{rad/s} \) about its center. Find \( K \).

Find \( I \) first, then use \( K = \tfrac12 I\omega^2 \).

\( I = \tfrac12(4.0)(0.30)^2 = 0.18\,\mathrm{kg{\cdot}m^2} \)

\( K = \tfrac12(0.18)(10)^2 = 9.0\,\mathrm{J} \)

B · Hoop vs. disk

A hoop and a disk, each \( 2.0\,\mathrm{kg} \) and \( R = 0.50\,\mathrm{m} \), both spin at \( 6.0\,\mathrm{rad/s} \).

Same \( \omega \), so compare \( I \).

disk: \( I = 0.25 \Rightarrow K = 4.5\,\mathrm{J} \)

hoop: \( I = 0.50 \Rightarrow K = 9.0\,\mathrm{J} \)

The hoop's mass is all at the rim, so it stores twice as much.

C · A rolling ball

A \( 6.0\,\mathrm{kg} \) solid ball (\( I = \tfrac25 MR^2 \)) rolls without slipping at \( 3.0\,\mathrm{m/s} \).

Use \( \omega = v/R \). Watch \( R \) cancel.

\( K_{\text{trans}} = \tfrac12(6.0)(3.0)^2 = 27\,\mathrm{J} \)

\( K_{\text{rot}} = \tfrac12\!\left(\tfrac25 MR^2\right)\!\tfrac{v^2}{R^2} = \tfrac15 Mv^2 = 10.8\,\mathrm{J} \)

\( K_{\text{tot}} = 37.8\,\mathrm{J} \)

1A ceiling fan has \( I = 0.80\,\mathrm{kg{\cdot}m^2} \) and spins at \( 5.0\,\mathrm{rad/s} \). How much rotational kinetic energy does it have?show the algebra
Plug straight in:

\( K = \tfrac12(0.80)(5.0)^2 \)

\( K = 10\,\mathrm{J} \)

2The same fan speeds up to \( 10\,\mathrm{rad/s} \). How many times bigger is its energy now?show the algebra
\( \omega \) doubled, and \( \omega \) is squared:

\( 2^2 = 4 \)

3A solid sphere and a hollow sphere have the same mass and radius and spin at the same \( \omega \). Which stores more energy, and by what factor?show the algebra
Same \( \omega \), so compare \( I \):

\( \dfrac{K_{\text{hollow}}}{K_{\text{solid}}} = \dfrac{\tfrac23 MR^2}{\tfrac25 MR^2} = \dfrac53 \)

Hollow sphere, about 1.7 times as much

Its mass sits out at the surface, far from the axis.
4A \( 2.0\,\mathrm{kg} \) solid cylinder rolls without slipping at \( 4.0\,\mathrm{m/s} \). What fraction of its kinetic energy is from spinning?show the algebra
For a cylinder, \( K_{\text{rot}} = \tfrac12(\tfrac12 MR^2)(v/R)^2 = \tfrac14 Mv^2 \):

\( K_{\text{trans}} = 16\,\mathrm{J},\; K_{\text{rot}} = 8\,\mathrm{J} \)

\( 8/24 = 1/3 \) of the total

5A solid sphere (\( 2.0\,\mathrm{kg} \), radius \( 0.15\,\mathrm{m} \), \( I = \tfrac25 mr^2 \)) spins at \( 5.0\,\mathrm{rad/s} \) about its center. Find its rotational kinetic energy.show the algebra

\( I = \tfrac25(2.0)(0.15)^2 = 0.018\,\mathrm{kg{\cdot}m^2} \)

\( K = \tfrac12(0.018)(5.0)^2 \)

\( K = 0.225\,\mathrm{J} \)

6A solid cylinder (\( 5.0\,\mathrm{kg} \), radius \( 0.10\,\mathrm{m} \), \( I = \tfrac12 mr^2 \)) rolls without slipping at \( 3.0\,\mathrm{m/s} \). Find its total kinetic energy.show the algebra
No slipping: \( \omega = v/r = 30\,\mathrm{rad/s} \), and \( I = 0.025\,\mathrm{kg{\cdot}m^2} \).

\( K_{\text{trans}} = \tfrac12(5.0)(3.0)^2 = 22.5\,\mathrm{J} \)

\( K_{\text{rot}} = \tfrac12(0.025)(30)^2 = 11.25\,\mathrm{J} \)

\( K_{\text{tot}} = 33.75\,\mathrm{J} \)

7A \( 1.0\,\mathrm{kg} \) solid sphere (\( r = 0.20\,\mathrm{m} \)) starts from rest at the top of a ramp \( 0.50\,\mathrm{m} \) high and rolls without slipping. What is its total kinetic energy at the bottom? How fast is it going?show the algebra
Static friction does no work, so all of \( mgh \) becomes kinetic energy.

\( K_{\text{tot}} = mgh = (1.0)(9.8)(0.50) = 4.9\,\mathrm{J} \)

For a solid sphere, \( K_{\text{tot}} = \tfrac12 mv^2 + \tfrac15 mv^2 = \tfrac{7}{10}mv^2 \):

\( v^2 = \tfrac{10gh}{7} = 7.0 \)

\( K_{\text{tot}} = 4.9\,\mathrm{J},\; v \approx 2.65\,\mathrm{m/s} \)

8Multiple choice. A space station with rotational inertia \( I_0 \) spins at \( \omega_0 \). It unfolds solar panels, so its rotational inertia becomes \( 2I_0 \). No outside torque acts. What happens to \( \omega \) and to \( K \)?(A) \( \omega \) same, \( K \) halves · (B) both stay the same · (C) \( \omega \) doubles, \( K \) same · (D) \( \omega \) halves, \( K \) halvesshow the answer
Sneak peek at 6.4: no outside torque means \( I\omega \) stays the same.

\( I_0\omega_0 = (2I_0)\,\omega_f \Rightarrow \omega_f = \tfrac12\omega_0 \)

\( K_f = \tfrac12(2I_0)\left(\tfrac{\omega_0}{2}\right)^2 = \tfrac12\left(\tfrac12 I_0\omega_0^2\right) \)

(D) \( \omega_f = \tfrac12\omega_0 \) and \( K_f = \tfrac12 K_0 \)

Topic 6.1 · summary

Pocket this.

1
**\( K = \tfrac12 I\omega^2 \)** is the spinning twin of \( K = \tfrac12 mv^2 \). It is measured in joules.
2
**\( I \) cares where the mass sits.** Mass far from the axis means a bigger \( I \) and more energy at the same \( \omega \).
3
**\( \omega \) is squared.** Double the spin rate and the energy becomes 4 times bigger.
4
**Something can spin with its center standing still** and still have kinetic energy.
5
**Rolling objects have both kinds:** \( K_{\text{tot}} = \tfrac12 Mv^2 + \tfrac12 I\omega^2 \). Energy is a scalar, so just add.

Topic 6.1 · Q&A

Questions people ask about spin energy.

If the center isn't moving, where does the energy come from?
Every bit of the object **except the axis** moves in a circle. Each bit has a speed, so each bit has \( \tfrac12 mv^2 \). Add them all up and you get \( \tfrac12 I\omega^2 \).
Does rotational kinetic energy have a direction?
No. Energy is a **scalar**. The spin itself can be clockwise or counterclockwise, but \( \tfrac12 I\omega^2 \) is always a positive number of joules.
Why does a hoop store more energy than a disk?
All of a hoop's mass sits on the rim, where things move fastest. A disk has lots of mass near the middle, moving slowly. Same \( M \) and \( R \), but the hoop's \( I \) is twice as big.
Do I have to memorize \( I = \tfrac25 MR^2 \) and friends?
Usually the problem gives you \( I \). Do remember the **ranking** for the same \( M \) and \( R \): hoop > hollow sphere > disk > solid sphere.
Can I use rpm or degrees per second?
Not in the formula. Convert to **rad/s** first: 1 turn = \( 2\pi \) rad and 1 minute = 60 s.
Can rotational kinetic energy be negative?
Never. \( I \) is positive and \( \omega^2 \) can't be negative. If you get a negative \( K \), check your algebra.

Topic 6.2 · the idea

A twist through an angle moves energy.

Loosen a bolt with a wrench. Your hand pushes with force \( F \), and the end of the wrench travels along an arc.

Work is force × distance. The arc length is \( s = r\Delta\theta \), so

\( W = F \cdot s = F \cdot r\Delta\theta = (rF)\,\Delta\theta = \tau\Delta\theta \)

τ in N·mΔθ in radiansW in joules

No turning means no work, even if you twist as hard as you can on a stuck bolt.

Unit 3

\[ W = F\Delta x \]

force × distance

⇄
Unit 6

\[ W = \tau\Delta\theta \]

torque × angle

Topic 6.2 · sign and graphs

Same way: energy in. Opposite way: energy out.

+
Torque with the turning. Pedaling a bike: the twist and the spin point the same way. \( W > 0 \), energy flows into the wheel and it speeds up.
−
Torque against the turning. A brake pad on a spinning wheel. \( W \lt 0 \), energy flows out and becomes heat in the pads.

Radians only! One turn is \( 2\pi \) rad. Plug in degrees and your answer is about 57 times too big.

Torque that changes as it turns

Use the graph. Work is the area under the \( \tau \)–\( \theta \) line: a rectangle for a steady torque, a triangle or trapezoid for one that changes evenly. Area below the axis counts as negative work.

Unit 3 graph

area under \( F \) vs. \( x \) = work

⇄
Unit 6 graph

area under \( \tau \) vs. \( \theta \) = work

Shade the area. That's the work.

Set the torque at the start and end of the turn, and how far it turns. Green area adds energy to the flywheel. Red area takes it away.

Topic 6.2 · work–energy theorem

Net work from torques changes spin energy.

Unit 3

\[ W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K = \tfrac12 mv_f^2 - \tfrac12 mv_i^2 \]

net work changes how fast it moves

⇄
Unit 6

\[ W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K_{\text{rot}} = \tfrac12 I\omega_f^2 - \tfrac12 I\omega_i^2 \]

net work changes how fast it spins

Example · potter's wheel

A potter's wheel (\( I = 2.0\,\mathrm{kg{\cdot}m^2} \)) starts at rest. A steady \( 6.0\,\mathrm{N{\cdot}m} \) torque turns it through 2 full turns. How fast is it spinning?

\( \Delta\theta = 2 \times 2\pi = 12.6\,\mathrm{rad} \)

\( W = (6.0)(12.6) = 75.4\,\mathrm{J} \)

\( 75.4 = \tfrac12(2.0)\,\omega^2 \Rightarrow \omega = 8.7\,\mathrm{rad/s} \)

This is the same bookkeeping as Unit 3. Torques that help add energy; torques that fight (brakes, axle friction) subtract it. Whatever is left over shows up as a change in \( \tfrac12 I\omega^2 \).

On an FRQ, say it in a chain: the torque acts through an angle → it does work → that work changes the rotational kinetic energy → so \( \omega \) goes up (or down).

Worked examples

Constant torque, a graph, and a brake.

A · Lug nut

A mechanic applies a steady \( 40\,\mathrm{N{\cdot}m} \) torque and the nut turns a quarter turn. How much work?

A quarter turn is \( \tfrac{\pi}{2} \) rad, not 90.

\( W = (40)(1.57) \)

\( W = 62.8\,\mathrm{J} \)

B · From a graph

Torque rises evenly from 0 to \( 12\,\mathrm{N{\cdot}m} \) over the first \( 2.0\,\mathrm{rad} \), then stays at \( 12\,\mathrm{N{\cdot}m} \) for \( 3.0\,\mathrm{rad} \) more.

Triangle + rectangle.

\( \tfrac12(2.0)(12) + (3.0)(12) \)

\( W = 12 + 36 = 48\,\mathrm{J} \)

C · How far to stop?

A grinding wheel has \( 90\,\mathrm{J} \) of spin energy. A brake applies \( 15\,\mathrm{N{\cdot}m} \) against the spin. How far does it turn before stopping?

All 90 J must leave: \( W = -90\,\mathrm{J} \).

\( -90 = -15\,\Delta\theta \)

\( \Delta\theta = 6.0\,\mathrm{rad} \approx 0.95 \) turn

8Multiple choice. A block of mass \( m \) hangs from a string wrapped around a heavy pulley of radius \( R \). It falls a distance \( h \) from rest. A student claims the string's torque does work \( mgh \) on the pulley. Best evaluation?(A) wrong: pulley work depends on fall distance, not inertia · (B) wrong: \( T \lt mg \), so less than \( mgh \) is done on the pulley · (C) right: all lost \( U \) goes to the pulley · (D) right: tension equals \( mg \)show the answer
The block speeds up on the way down, so the net force on it is downward: \( mg - T = ma > 0 \).

\( T \lt mg \Rightarrow W_{\text{pulley}} = TR\,\Delta\theta = Th \lt mgh \)

(B)

The rest of \( mgh \) becomes the block's own kinetic energy.

Topic 6.2 · summary

Pocket this.

1
**\( W = \tau\Delta\theta \)** is the spinning twin of \( W = F\Delta x \). Angle in **radians**, work in joules.
2
**The sign tells the story.** Torque with the turning: energy in (+). Torque against the turning: energy out (−).
3
**No turning, no work**, no matter how big the torque.
4
**Graph rule:** work = area under the \( \tau \)–\( \theta \) line. Rectangles, triangles, trapezoids.
5
**\( W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K_{\text{rot}} \)**: net work from torques changes how fast something spins.

Topic 6.2 · Q&A

Questions people ask about torque and work.

Why must the angle be in radians?
The arc length rule \( s = r\Delta\theta \) only works in radians. That rule is what turns \( \tau\Delta\theta \) into force × distance, which is joules.
Torque is N·m and work is J = N·m. Are they the same thing?
Same units, different ideas. Torque is a **twist**; work is **energy moved**. Write torque in N·m and work in J so nobody mixes them up.
Can the work done by a torque be negative?
Yes, whenever the torque points against the turning: brakes, axle friction, or you slowing down a merry-go-round.
What if the torque keeps changing?
Draw (or read) the \( \tau \)–\( \theta \) graph and find the **area** under it.
How is this different from Unit 5?
Unit 5: \( \tau_{\text{net}} = I\alpha \) says how **quickly** the spin changes. Unit 6: \( \tau\Delta\theta \) says how much **energy** moves, and \( \tau\Delta t \) (topic 6.3) says how much **momentum** moves.
Where does the energy go when a brake stops a wheel?
Into **thermal energy**: the brake pads and wheel rim warm up. Total energy is still conserved; it just isn't kinetic anymore.

Topic 6.3 · angular momentum

Spin has momentum too.

A heavy bike wheel spinning fast is hard to stop and hard to tilt. It carries a lot of "spin." Physicists call that angular momentum, \( L \).

Two things make \( L \) big: lots of rotational inertia (mass far from the axis) and a fast spin rate.

units kg·m²/s+ counterclockwise− clockwise

Try it: spin a fidget spinner, then try to tilt it. It fights you. That's angular momentum at work.

Straight line · Unit 4

\[ p = mv \]

how hard it is to stop something moving

⇅
Spinning · Unit 6

\[ L = I\omega \]

how hard it is to stop something spinning

AP Physics 1 only uses + and − signs for \( L \). Its 3-D arrow direction is beyond the course.

Topic 6.3 · L about a point

Even something moving in a straight line can have \( L \).

Pick a point P. A puck slides past it. Measured from P, the puck has angular momentum

\[ L = r\,m\,v\sin\theta \]

  • r
    distance from P to the object
  • θ
    angle between \( \vec r \) and the velocity
  • d
    \( r\sin\theta \) is just the "miss distance": how far the path passes from P. So \( L = mvd \).
Unit 5 twin

\[ \tau = rF\sin\theta \]

force × lever arm

⇅
Unit 6

\[ L = r(mv)\sin\theta \]

momentum × lever arm

Change the point and you change \( L \). Always say which point or axis you measured from. \( L = 0 \) only if the path runs straight through P.

Topic 6.3 · angular impulse

A twist that lasts a while changes \( L \).

Push a merry-go-round for 3 seconds and it spins up. Twist harder, or longer, and you add more spin.

Start from Newton's second law for spinning (Unit 5):

\( \tau_{\text{net}} = I\alpha = I\dfrac{\Delta\omega}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{\Delta L}{\Delta t} \;\Rightarrow\; \tau\Delta t = \Delta L \)

  • ∫
    Area under a \( \tau \)–\( t \) graph = angular impulse = \( \Delta L \).
  • ∕
    Slope of an \( L \)–\( t \) graph = net torque.
Unit 4 twin

\[ F\Delta t = \Delta p \]

impulse changes momentum

⇅
Unit 6

\[ \tau\Delta t = \Delta L \]

angular impulse changes angular momentum

units N·m·s = kg·m²/ssign same as the torque

Worked examples

A spinning platform, a passing ball, and a motor.

A · Merry-go-round

A merry-go-round has \( I = 250\,\mathrm{kg{\cdot}m^2} \) and spins at \( 1.2\,\mathrm{rad/s} \). Find \( L \).

Rigid object spinning about its axis → \( L = I\omega \).

\( L = (250)(1.2) \)

\( L = 300\,\mathrm{kg{\cdot}m^2/s} \)

B · A ball passing a post

A \( 0.40\,\mathrm{kg} \) ball moves at \( 5.0\,\mathrm{m/s} \) in a straight line that misses a post by \( 0.60\,\mathrm{m} \). Find \( L \) about the post.

Point object → \( L = rmv\sin\theta = mvd \).

\( L = (0.40)(5.0)(0.60) \)

\( L = 1.2\,\mathrm{kg{\cdot}m^2/s} \)

C · Motor spin-up

A wheel (\( I = 0.50\,\mathrm{kg{\cdot}m^2} \)) already spins at \( 6.0\,\mathrm{rad/s} \). A motor adds \( 4.0\,\mathrm{N{\cdot}m} \) in the same direction for \( 2.5\,\mathrm{s} \).

\( L_0 = (0.50)(6.0) = 3.0 \)

\( \Delta L = (4.0)(2.5) = 10 \)

\( \omega = \tfrac{13}{0.50} = 26\,\mathrm{rad/s} \)

\( \tau = \tfrac{9.0}{3.0} = 3.0\,\mathrm{N{\cdot}m} \)

8Multiple choice. Disk A (radius \( R \)) and disk B (radius \( 2R \)) are made of the same material, same thickness, and are linked by a belt that doesn't slip. How does \( L_B \) compare with \( L_A \)?(A) \( 8L_A \) · (B) \( 2L_A \) · (C) \( 4L_A \) · (D) \( 16L_A \)show the answer
Twice the radius → 4 times the area → \( M_B = 4M_A \).

\( I_B = \tfrac12(4M)(2R)^2 = 16\,I_A \)

The belt gives both rims the same speed, so \( \omega_B = \tfrac12\omega_A \).

\( L_B = (16I_A)(\tfrac12\omega_A) \)

Topic 6.3 · summary

Pocket this.

1
**\( L = I\omega \)** for a spinning object: the twin of \( p = mv \).
2
**\( L = rmv\sin\theta \)** for an object moving past a point, even in a straight line. The value depends on the point you pick.
3
**\( \tau\Delta t = \Delta L \)**: a twist that lasts a while changes the spin, the twin of \( F\Delta t = \Delta p \).
4
**Graphs:** area under \( \tau \)–\( t \) = \( \Delta L \). Slope of \( L \)–\( t \) = net torque.
5
**Signs, not 3-D arrows.** Use + for counterclockwise and − for clockwise.

Topic 6.3 · Q&A

Questions people ask about angular momentum.

What's the difference between angular impulse and angular momentum?
Angular impulse \( \tau\Delta t \) is the **cause** (a twist over time). The change in angular momentum \( \Delta L \) is the **result**. They are equal in size.
Why does the point I pick matter?
\( r \) and \( \theta \) are measured from that point. Pick a different point and the numbers change. Choose one, say it, and stick with it for the whole problem.
How can something moving in a straight line have angular momentum?
Watch it from a point off to the side: the line from you to the object sweeps around. Only if the path goes **through** your point is \( L = 0 \).
Is \( \tau_{\text{net}} = I\alpha \) still true?
Yes, when \( I \) stays the same. \( \tau_{\text{net}} = \Delta L/\Delta t \) is the bigger rule; it still works when \( I \) changes, like a skater pulling her arms in.
Does a bigger torque always mean a bigger change in \( L \)?
Not by itself. \( \Delta L \) depends on torque **and** time. A small torque for a long time can match a big torque for a short time.
Are N·m·s and kg·m²/s really the same?
Yes. A newton is kg·m/s², so N·m·s = kg·m²/s. That's why \( \tau\Delta t \) can equal \( \Delta L \).

Topic 6.4 · the rule

No outside twist? The total spin can't change.

Add up the angular momentum of every part of a system, all measured about the same axis. If nothing outside the system twists it, that total stays the same forever.

\( L_{\text{total}} = L_1 + L_2 + L_3 + \dots \)

When a system changes shape, this becomes

\[ I_1\omega_1 = I_2\omega_2 \]

before = after

Unit 4 twin

\[ \Sigma F_{\text{ext}} = 0 \Rightarrow p_i = p_f \]

no outside push, momentum stays put

⇅
Unit 6

\[ \Sigma \tau_{\text{ext}} = 0 \Rightarrow L_i = L_f \]

no outside twist, spin stays put

Pull mass in → \( I \) shrinks → \( \omega \) grows. Push mass out → \( I \) grows → \( \omega \) shrinks.

Topic 6.4 · system choice

Your system decides what counts as "outside."

When two parts twist each other, the twists are equal and opposite (Newton's third law). Inside one system they cancel, so they can't change the total \( L \).

SituationSystem you pickTwist between the parts is…Is the system's \( L \) constant?
Student on a stool pulls in two weightsstudent aloneoutsidenot necessarily
student + stool + weightsinsideyes, if axle friction is tiny
Ball hits a pivoted rod and sticksball aloneoutsideno: the rod's twist changes it
ball + rodinsideyes, about the pivot

Pick a bigger system and outside twists become inside twists. That's often the trick that unlocks conservation.

If an outside torque does act, \( L \) changes by the angular impulse: \( \Delta L = \tau_{\text{ext}}\Delta t \). Spin flows in or out.

Topic 6.4 · collisions

In a spinning collision, \( L \) survives. Kinetic energy doesn't.

The pivot pushes on the rod during the hit, but that push acts at the axis. Its lever arm is zero, so its torque is zero. Angular momentum about the pivot survives the collision.

before: \( L = m v \ell \) (ball only)

after: \( L = (I_{\text{rod}} + m\ell^2)\,\omega_f \)

Unit 4 twin · sticky collision

\[ m_1v_1 = (m_1+m_2)\,v_f \]

⇅
Unit 6 · sticky spin collision

\[ mv\ell = (I_{\text{rod}} + m\ell^2)\,\omega_f \]

Just like a sticky collision in Unit 4, some kinetic energy turns into heat and sound. Use angular momentum, not energy, to find \( \omega_f \).

Worked examples

A stool, two disks, and a running kid.

A · Spinning stool

A student on a stool (\( I = 5.0\,\mathrm{kg{\cdot}m^2} \)) spins at \( 1.5\,\mathrm{rad/s} \), then pulls in so \( I = 2.0 \).

\( (5.0)(1.5) = (2.0)\,\omega_2 \)

\( \omega_2 = 3.75\,\mathrm{rad/s} \)

\( K \) goes from 5.6 J to 14.1 J. The extra came from her arm muscles.

B · Disks lock together

Disk 1 (\( I = 0.40 \)) spinning at \( 30\,\mathrm{rad/s} \) drops onto disk 2 (\( I = 0.20 \)), at rest on the same axle. They stick.

\( (0.40)(30) = (0.60)\,\omega_f \)

\( \omega_f = 20\,\mathrm{rad/s} \)

\( K \): 180 J → 120 J. The rubbing disks made 60 J of heat.

C · Kid jumps on

A platform (\( I = 300 \), \( R = 2.0\,\mathrm{m} \)) is at rest. A \( 30\,\mathrm{kg} \) kid running \( 4.0\,\mathrm{m/s} \) along the edge jumps on at the rim.

\( L = (30)(4.0)(2.0) = 240 \)

\( I_f = 300 + 30(2.0)^2 = 420 \)

\( \omega_f = 240/420 = 0.57\,\mathrm{rad/s} \)

6A student on a low-friction stool has \( I = 3.0\,\mathrm{kg{\cdot}m^2} \) and spins at \( 2.4\,\mathrm{rad/s} \). Pulling masses inward makes \( I = 2.0 \). New spin rate?show the algebra

7A rod (\( \ell = 2.0\,\mathrm{m} \), \( 0.5\,\mathrm{kg} \), \( I = \tfrac13 m\ell^2 \)) hangs from a pivot at one end. A \( 0.2\,\mathrm{kg} \) ball moving \( 15\,\mathrm{m/s} \) at right angles to the rod hits the free end and sticks. Find \( \omega \) just after.show the algebra
System: rod + ball, about the pivot. The pivot force acts at the axis, so no outside torque.

\( L_i = mv\ell = (0.2)(15)(2.0) = 6.0\,\mathrm{kg{\cdot}m^2/s} \)

Topic 6.4 · summary

Pocket this.

1
**No net outside torque → \( L_i = L_f \).** The spinning twin of momentum conservation.
2
**Shape changes:** \( I_1\omega_1 = I_2\omega_2 \). Smaller \( I \) means a faster spin.
3
**Inside twists cancel** (Newton's third law). Choosing a bigger system can turn outside twists into inside ones.
4
**\( L \) conserved does not mean \( K \) conserved.** Pulling arms in adds \( K \); sticky collisions lose \( K \).
5
**Forces at the pivot make no torque about the pivot**, so use \( L \) about the pivot in collisions.

Topic 6.4 · Q&A

Questions people ask about conservation.

Where does the skater's extra kinetic energy come from?
Her **arm muscles**. Pulling the weights inward takes work, and that work becomes extra rotational kinetic energy.
Gravity pulls on the skater. Isn't that an outside torque?
Gravity and the push of the ice act along her vertical spin axis, so their lever arm is zero. No torque about that axis.
Is linear momentum conserved when a kid jumps on a merry-go-round?
No. The axle pushes on the platform, which is an outside **force**. But that force acts at the axis, so it makes no **torque**, and \( L \) about the axle is conserved.
Why do divers and gymnasts tuck?
Tucking shrinks \( I \), so they spin faster and fit more flips in the air. Opening up before landing slows the spin.
What about friction in the axle?
It's an outside torque. During a quick collision it barely matters. Over a long time it slowly drains \( L \), which is why a merry-go-round eventually stops.
Can I add \( L \) values measured about different axes?
No. Every part must be measured about the **same axis** before you add.

Topic 6.5 · the idea

Rolling is sliding and spinning, locked together.

When a wheel rolls without slipping, the spin speed at the rim exactly cancels the slide at the bottom. The contact point is at rest for an instant. One full turn moves the wheel forward one full circumference.

Unit 5

\[ v = r\omega \]

a point on a spinning wheel

⇄
Unit 6 · rolling

\[ v_{\text{cm}} = r\omega \]

also \( a_{\text{cm}} = r\alpha \), \( \Delta x_{\text{cm}} = r\Delta\theta \)

Topic 6.5 · energy

Same hill, different shapes, different speeds.

Write \( I = \beta MR^2 \), where \( \beta \) is a shape number (hoop 1, disk ½, solid sphere ⅖). Rolling from rest down a height \( h \):

\( Mgh = \tfrac12 Mv^2 + \tfrac12(\beta MR^2)\left(\tfrac{v}{R}\right)^2 = \tfrac12 Mv^2(1+\beta) \)

\[ v = \sqrt{\frac{2gh}{1+\beta}} \]

\( M \) and \( R \) cancel. Only the shape matters.

Slides, no friction

\[ v = \sqrt{2gh} \]

⇄
Rolls

\[ v = \sqrt{\tfrac{2gh}{1+\beta}} \]

From a 1.0 m high ramp

Racer\( \beta \)speed at bottomenergy in spin
Sliding cart04.43 m/s0%
Solid sphere⅖3.74 m/s29%
Solid disk½3.61 m/s33%
Hollow sphere⅔3.43 m/s40%
Hoop13.13 m/s50%

The more energy a shape spends on spinning, the less is left for moving forward.

Topic 6.5 · friction

Static friction rolls for free. Kinetic friction charges a fee.

✓
Rolling without slipping. Static friction acts at the contact point, which isn't sliding. It supplies the twist that spins the ball up, but it does no work. Mechanical energy is conserved.
✗
Rolling while slipping. A skidding bowling ball or a spinning tire. Now \( v_{\text{cm}} \ne r\omega \), kinetic friction rubs, and some energy becomes heat.

AP boundary: slipping is described in words only, with no equations. Rolling friction is not on the exam.

?College Board ranking task. A wheel rolls from rest down a ramp onto flat ground on three tracks: (1) rough, no slipping; (2) some friction, but it slips; (3) no friction at all. Rank the wheel's \( K_{\text{trans}} \), \( K_{\text{rot}} \), and total energy at the end.show the answer

\( K_{\text{trans}}:\; 3 > 2 > 1 \)

\( K_{\text{rot}}:\; 1 > 2 > 3 \)

\( E_{\text{total}}:\; 1 = 3 > 2 \)

Track 3: nothing twists the wheel, so it never spins. All energy goes into sliding, none is lost. Track 1: energy splits between sliding and spinning, none is lost. Track 2: it spins some, but kinetic friction turns part of the energy into heat, so it ends with the least.

Worked examples

A ramp, an energy split, and a tire.

A · Speed at the bottom

A solid ball (\( \beta = \tfrac25 \)) rolls from rest down a ramp \( 1.4\,\mathrm{m} \) high. How fast at the bottom?

\( v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2(9.8)(1.4)}{1.4}} \)

\( v = \sqrt{19.6} = 4.4\,\mathrm{m/s} \)

B · Energy split

A \( 1.5\,\mathrm{kg} \) hoop (\( I = MR^2 \)) rolls at \( 2.0\,\mathrm{m/s} \). Split its kinetic energy.

\( K_{\text{trans}} = \tfrac12(1.5)(2.0)^2 = 3.0\,\mathrm{J} \)

\( K_{\text{rot}} = \tfrac12(MR^2)\tfrac{v^2}{R^2} = 3.0\,\mathrm{J} \)

A hoop always splits 50/50.

C · Tire turns

A tire of radius \( 0.30\,\mathrm{m} \) rolls 100 turns without slipping. How far does the car go? At \( 12\,\mathrm{m/s} \), what is \( \omega \)?

\( \Delta x = r\Delta\theta = (0.30)(200\pi) = 188\,\mathrm{m} \)

\( \omega = v/r = 12/0.30 = 40\,\mathrm{rad/s} \)

5A solid sphere (\( 2.0\,\mathrm{kg} \), radius \( 10\,\mathrm{cm} \)) rolls without slipping at \( 5.0\,\mathrm{m/s} \). Find its total kinetic energy.show the algebra

\( \omega = 5.0/0.10 = 50\,\mathrm{rad/s},\quad I = \tfrac25(2.0)(0.10)^2 = 0.008 \)

\( K_{\text{trans}} = \tfrac12(2.0)(5.0)^2 = 25.0\,\mathrm{J},\quad K_{\text{rot}} = \tfrac12(0.008)(50)^2 = 10.0\,\mathrm{J} \)

6A solid cylinder (\( 5.0\,\mathrm{kg} \), radius \( 20\,\mathrm{cm} \)) starts from rest on a 30° ramp and rolls without slipping. How fast is it moving after dropping \( 2.0\,\mathrm{m} \) vertically?show the algebra
The angle doesn't matter for energy; only the height drop does.

\( mgh = \tfrac12 mv^2 + \tfrac12(\tfrac12 mr^2)(v/r)^2 = \tfrac34 mv^2 \)

\( v = \sqrt{4gh/3} \approx 5.1\,\mathrm{m/s} \)

7A \( 7.2\,\mathrm{kg} \) bowling ball (radius \( 10.8\,\mathrm{cm} \)) sits on a flat floor. A \( 10\,\mathrm{N} \) horizontal push acts at its center. How much static friction is needed for it to roll without slipping?show the algebra
Three equations: sliding, spinning, and the no-slip link.

\( F - f_s = ma,\quad f_s r = \tfrac25 mr^2\alpha,\quad a = r\alpha \)

\( f_s = \tfrac25 ma = \tfrac25(F - f_s) \Rightarrow 7f_s = 2F \)

\( f_s = \tfrac27(10) \approx 2.86\,\mathrm{N} \)

Topic 6.5 · summary

Pocket this.

1
**No-slip link:** \( v_{\text{cm}} = r\omega \), \( a_{\text{cm}} = r\alpha \), \( \Delta x_{\text{cm}} = r\Delta\theta \). The contact point is at rest for an instant.
2
**Never forget the spin part:** \( K_{\text{tot}} = \tfrac12 Mv^2 + \tfrac12 I\omega^2 \).
3
**Down a ramp, shape decides.** Mass and radius cancel. Smaller \( \beta = I/MR^2 \) means faster.
4
**Static friction (no slip): no energy lost. Kinetic friction (slipping): energy turns into heat.**
5
**Slipping is explained in words only** on AP Physics 1.

Topic 6.5 · Q&A

Questions people ask about rolling.

If friction acts, how is energy conserved?
Static friction acts at a point that **isn't sliding**, so it does no work. No rubbing means no heating.
Why is the top of a wheel faster than its center?
The spin adds \( r\omega \) forward at the top and \( r\omega \) backward at the bottom. Add the forward slide \( v \): top \( 2v \), center \( v \), bottom 0.
Does a heavier ball roll down faster?
Not if it's the same shape: mass cancels. A solid ball beats a hollow ball no matter which is heavier.
What happens on a perfectly icy ramp?
Nothing twists the ball, so it never starts spinning. It slides like a block and reaches \( \sqrt{2gh} \), faster than any roller.
Why does slipping waste energy?
The contact point rubs along the ground, so kinetic friction does negative work. That energy turns into heat.
Do I need an equation for rolling while slipping?
No. The exact math is beyond AP Physics 1. Be ready to explain **in words** what speeds up, what slows down, and where energy goes.

Topic 6.6 · the idea

A satellite is a ball that keeps missing the ground.

Throw a ball sideways and it curves down to the ground. Throw it faster and it lands farther away. Throw it fast enough and the ground curves away as fast as the ball falls. It never lands. That's an orbit.

  • 1
    Big planet, tiny satellite. The planet barely moves, so we treat it as standing still. Think bowling ball and marble on a trampoline.
  • 2
    Only gravity acts. It pulls toward the planet's center, so it makes no torque about the center: \( L \) stays constant.
  • 3
    Gravity doesn't waste energy, so the total mechanical energy \( E \) stays constant too.
Projectile · Units 1 & 3

\[ K + mgh = \text{constant} \]

only gravity, near the ground

⇅
Satellite · Unit 6

\[ K - \frac{GMm}{r} = \text{constant} \]

only gravity, far from the ground, and \( L \) is constant too

Topic 6.6 · potential energy

Far from a planet, gravitational energy is negative.

It's like a well. Being deep in the well (close) means very negative energy. To climb all the way out, you must add energy until \( U \) reaches zero.

\[ U_g = -\frac{Gm_1m_2}{r} \]

\( r \) = center-to-center distance, not height above the ground

Near the ground

\[ U = mgh \]

a zoomed-in slice of the big curve

⇅
Anywhere

\[ U_g = -\tfrac{GMm}{r} \]

zero at infinity

e.g. 1000 kg at \( 7.0\times10^6\,\mathrm{m} \): \( U_g = -5.7\times10^{10}\,\mathrm{J} \)

Topic 6.6 · orbit shapes

Circle or ellipse: what stays the same?

QuantityCircular orbitElliptical orbit
distance \( r \)constantchanges
speed and \( K \)constantchanges
\( U_g \)constantchanges
total energy \( E \)constantconstant
angular momentum \( L \)constantconstant

In an ellipse, \( K \) and \( U_g \) trade back and forth, like a roller coaster trading height for speed.

At the closest and farthest points the velocity is sideways to \( r \), so \( L = mrv \) there, and

\( r_p v_p = r_a v_a \)

That's why planets speed up near the Sun: smaller \( r \), so bigger \( v \) to keep \( L \) the same.

Topic 6.6 · escape speed

Escape speed: total energy exactly zero.

\( E = \tfrac12 mv^2 - \dfrac{GMm}{r} \)

To barely escape, the rocket coasts out to "infinity" and arrives with zero speed. There, \( K = 0 \) and \( U = 0 \), so \( E = 0 \). Energy is conserved, so \( E = 0 \) at launch too:

\( \tfrac12 mv_{\text{esc}}^2 = \dfrac{GMm}{r} \)

\[ v_{\text{esc}} = \sqrt{\frac{2GM}{r}} \]

the rocket's mass \( m \) cancels

E < 0 stuck: falls back or orbitsE = 0 just escapesE > 0 escapes with speed to spare

Worked examples

An ellipse, the Moon, and a probe.

A · Speeds in an ellipse

At its closest point (\( 7.0\times10^6\,\mathrm{m} \)) a satellite moves \( 8.0\,\mathrm{km/s} \). Its farthest point is \( 1.4\times10^7\,\mathrm{m} \). Speed there?

\( r_pv_p = r_av_a \)

\( v_a = \tfrac{(7.0)(8.0)}{14} = 4.0\,\mathrm{km/s} \)

B · Escape from the Moon

\( M = 7.35\times10^{22}\,\mathrm{kg} \), \( R = 1.74\times10^6\,\mathrm{m} \).

\( v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2(6.67\times10^{-11})(7.35\times10^{22})}{1.74\times10^6}} \)

\( v \approx 2.4\,\mathrm{km/s} \)

C · Will it come back?

A \( 500\,\mathrm{kg} \) probe is \( 1.0\times10^7\,\mathrm{m} \) from Earth's center, moving \( 8.0\,\mathrm{km/s} \).

\( K = 1.60\times10^{10}\,\mathrm{J} \)

\( U = -1.99\times10^{10}\,\mathrm{J} \)

\( E = -3.9\times10^{9}\,\mathrm{J} \lt 0 \): it's stuck

Your turn. What stays, what changes?

Original practice Decide what's constant first, then use it.

Remember\( U_g = -\tfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r} \)\( r_pv_p = r_av_a \)\( v_{\text{esc}} = \sqrt{2GM/r} \)
1A satellite is in a circular orbit. Which of these stay constant: speed, \( K \), \( U_g \), \( E \), \( L \)?show the answer

All five

The distance never changes, so nothing else has a reason to change.
2In an elliptical orbit, the farthest point is 3 times as far from the planet as the closest point. Compare the speeds there.show the algebra

\( r_pv_p = (3r_p)\,v_a \)

\( v_a = \tfrac13 v_p \)

3You double the mass of a rocket. What happens to the escape speed it needs?show the answer

Nothing

\( m \) cancels in \( \tfrac12 mv^2 = GMm/r \). A pebble and a spaceship need the same speed.
4A planet has Earth's mass but half its radius. Escape speed from its surface?show the algebra
\( v \propto 1/\sqrt{r} \), so halving \( r \) multiplies \( v \) by \( \sqrt2 \):

\( 11.2\sqrt2 \approx 15.8\,\mathrm{km/s} \)

Practice · 6.6 · study guide

Four problems from the Fiveable 6.6 guide.

From the Fiveable guide Problems reworded; solutions written step by step for this deck.

5A satellite follows an elliptical orbit. Which quantities stay constant all the way around, and which change?show the answer

Constant: total energy \( E \) and angular momentum \( L \)

Changing: kinetic energy (speed) and gravitational potential energy (distance). Fastest when closest, slowest when farthest.
6A \( 1500\,\mathrm{kg} \) satellite orbits \( 42\,000\,\mathrm{km} \) from Earth's center (\( M = 5.97\times10^{24}\,\mathrm{kg} \)). Find the system's gravitational potential energy.show the algebra
Use the center-to-center distance, in meters: \( 4.2\times10^7\,\mathrm{m} \).

\( U_g = -\dfrac{(6.67\times10^{-11})(5.97\times10^{24})(1500)}{4.2\times10^7} \)

\( U_g \approx -1.42\times10^{10}\,\mathrm{J} \)

7Find the escape speed from the surface of Mars (\( M = 6.42\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{kg} \), \( R = 3390\,\mathrm{km} \)).show the algebra

\( v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2(6.67\times10^{-11})(6.42\times10^{23})}{3.39\times10^6}} \)

\( v \approx 5.03\,\mathrm{km/s} \)

Less than half of Earth's 11.2 km/s, so leaving Mars takes much less fuel.
8Multiple choice. A satellite moves from a circular orbit of radius \( r_1 \) to one of radius \( r_2 = 2r_1 \). Compare its \( K \) and the system's \( E \).(A) \( K_2 > K_1,\, E_2 > E_1 \) · (B) \( K_2 \lt K_1,\, E_2 > E_1 \) · (C) \( K_2 > K_1,\, E_2 \lt E_1 \) · (D) \( K_2 \lt K_1,\, E_2 \lt E_1 \)show the answer
Gravity supplies the circular-motion force: \( \tfrac{GMm}{r^2} = \tfrac{mv^2}{r} \), so \( K = \tfrac{GMm}{2r} \).

\( E = K + U = \tfrac{GMm}{2r} - \tfrac{GMm}{r} = -\tfrac{GMm}{2r} \)

Doubling \( r \) halves \( K \) and makes \( E \) half as negative, which is bigger.

(B) \( K_2 \lt K_1 \) and \( E_2 > E_1 \)

Topic 6.6 · summary

Pocket this.

1
**Only gravity acts**, so a satellite's total energy \( E \) and angular momentum \( L \) never change. The planet's own motion is negligible.
2
**Circle: everything is constant. Ellipse: \( K \) and \( U_g \) trade**, fastest at the closest point.
3
**\( U_g = -\tfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r} \)**: zero at infinity, more negative when closer. Use center-to-center \( r \).
4
**Escape means \( E = 0 \)**, so \( v_{\text{esc}} = \sqrt{2GM/r} \). The satellite's mass cancels.

Topic 6.6 · Q&A

Questions people ask about orbits.

Why is gravitational potential energy negative?
We chose **zero at infinity**. Anything closer sits "below" zero: you'd have to add energy to pull it all the way out.
Why doesn't a satellite fall down?
It **is** falling, all the time. It just moves sideways so fast that the ground curves away beneath it.
Why is angular momentum conserved in an orbit?
Gravity points straight at the planet's center, so its lever arm about the center is zero. No torque means \( L \) can't change.
Is \( mgh \) wrong, then?
No. It's a great approximation for small heights near the surface. For orbits and escapes, use \( -GMm/r \).
Does the escape direction matter?
Ignoring air, no. Energy is a scalar, so any direction that doesn't hit the planet works.
At escape speed, does it zoom away forever?
It keeps slowing down as it climbs. At exactly \( v_{\text{esc}} \) its speed reaches zero only at infinity.

Tap a question to see the answer.

Everything on one wall

Every Unit 6 equation, next to its straight-line twin.

6.1 · spin energy

\[ K_{\text{rot}} = \tfrac12 I\omega^2 \]

twin: \( K = \tfrac12 mv^2 \)

6.1 · 6.5 · move + spin

\[ K_{\text{tot}} = K_{\text{trans}} + K_{\text{rot}} \]

\( \tfrac12 Mv_{\text{cm}}^2 + \tfrac12 I\omega^2 \); scalars just add

6.2 · work by a torque

\[ W = \tau\Delta\theta \]

twin: \( W = F\Delta x \) · area under \( \tau \)–\( \theta \)

6.2 · work–energy

\[ W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K_{\text{rot}} \]

twin: \( W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K \)

6.3 · angular momentum

\[ L = I\omega \]

twin: \( p = mv \)

6.3 · object about a point

\[ L = rmv\sin\theta \]

twin: \( \tau = rF\sin\theta \) (lever-arm idea)

6.3 · angular impulse

\[ \tau\Delta t = \Delta L \]

twin: \( F\Delta t = \Delta p \) · area under \( \tau \)–\( t \)

6.3 · Newton 2, spinning

\[ \tau_{\text{net}} = \frac{\Delta L}{\Delta t} = I\alpha \]

twin: \( F_{\text{net}} = \frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t} = ma \) · slope of \( L \)–\( t \)

6.4 · conservation

\[ I_1\omega_1 = I_2\omega_2 \]

if \( \tau_{\text{ext}} = 0 \) · twin: \( p_i = p_f \) if \( F_{\text{ext}} = 0 \)

6.5 · rolling link

\[ v_{\text{cm}} = r\omega \]

\( a_{\text{cm}} = r\alpha \), \( \Delta x_{\text{cm}} = r\Delta\theta \) (no slipping)

6.6 · gravity energy

\[ U_g = -\frac{Gm_1m_2}{r} \]

twin near the ground: \( U = mgh \)

6.6 · escape

\[ v_{\text{esc}} = \sqrt{\frac{2GM}{r}} \]

from \( E = \tfrac12 mv^2 - \tfrac{GMm}{r} = 0 \)

The AP workflow

Five steps for any Unit 6 problem.

1

Draw the system

What's inside it, where the axis is, and which way is + (usually counterclockwise).

2

Check the outside

Outside torque? Then \( L \) changes. Sliding friction? Then mechanical energy leaks out as heat.

3

Pick the tool

Use the chart below. Rolling without slipping? Add \( v = r\omega \).

4

Symbols first

Start from a law you can name. Solve with letters, plug in numbers last.

5

Check and explain

Units, signs, size. Then write the chain: law → this system → claim.

If the problem gives you…Reach for…
heights, speeds, "from rest", ramps, orbitsEnergy: \( K_i + U_i + W_{\text{other}} = K_f + U_f \), with \( K = \tfrac12 Mv^2 + \tfrac12 I\omega^2 \)
arms pulled in, objects sticking, "no outside torque"Angular momentum: \( L_i = L_f \)
a time interval, or a \( \tau \)–\( t \) graphAngular impulse: \( \tau\Delta t = \Delta L \)
an angle turned, or a \( \tau \)–\( \theta \) graphWork: \( W = \tau\Delta\theta \), then \( W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K \)
"how does X change if Y doubles?"Write the equation, hold the rest constant, read off the factor

Writing for the free-response section

Naming a law isn't enough. Walk the chain.

Prompt: a hoop and a solid disk with the same mass and radius roll from rest down the same ramp. Which reaches the bottom first? Justify.

Earns little

"The disk wins because of conservation of energy."

It names a law but never connects it to the hoop or the disk. The College Board says this is not a complete answer.

Earns full credit
  1. Law: both start with the same \( Mgh \), and static friction does no work, so each ends with \( K_{\text{tot}} = Mgh \).
  2. Apply it: \( K_{\text{tot}} = \tfrac12 Mv^2 + \tfrac12 I\omega^2 \) with \( \omega = v/R \).
  3. What's different: the hoop's mass is all at the rim, so its \( I \) is bigger and more of \( Mgh \) goes into spinning.
  4. Claim: less energy is left for \( \tfrac12 Mv^2 \), so the hoop is slower at every height. The disk arrives first.

Pattern: name the law → apply it to this system → say what's different → finish with the claim.

Free-response practice

Three FRQ-style setups from the Fiveable Unit 6 page.

From the Fiveable unit page Setups condensed; answers written for this deck. Try each part before you open it.

AExperimental design. A disk on a low-friction axle is spun up by a string on a small spool (\( r = 0.0200\,\mathrm{m} \)). The string runs over a pulley to a \( 0.200\,\mathrm{kg} \) hanging mass. After falling for time \( t \), the string is stopped and a photogate reads \( \omega \). Data: \( (0.40\,\mathrm{s}, 8.2) \), \( (0.60, 12.0) \), \( (0.80, 15.9) \), \( (1.00, 20.4) \), \( (1.20, 24.1\,\mathrm{rad/s}) \). What should you graph, and what is \( I \)?show the answer
From rest with a steady torque, \( \omega = (\tau/I)\,t \). Graph \( \omega \) (vertical) against \( t \): the slope is \( \tau/I \).

\( \tau = mgr = (0.200)(9.80)(0.0200) = 0.0392\,\mathrm{N{\cdot}m} \)

slope from the best-fit points \( (0.40, 8.0) \) and \( (1.20, 24.0) \): \( \tfrac{16.0}{0.80} = 20.0\,\mathrm{rad/s^2} \)

\( I = \tau/\text{slope} \approx 1.96\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{kg{\cdot}m^2} \)

Add a second identical disk and \( I \) doubles, so the slope halves. Note that \( \tau = mgr \) runs slightly high because the falling mass accelerates (\( T \lt mg \)), so repeat trials and keep the fall short.
BMathematical routines. A disk and a ring are glued together and spin on a frictionless vertical axle. A force \( F \), always tangent to the ring's outer rim (radius \( R \)), acts from \( t = 0 \) to \( t_1 \) while the system turns through \( \theta_1 \). Sketch \( \tau_{\text{net}} \) vs. \( t \), find the angular impulse and the work, and say what happens to \( L \).show the answer
The torque is a constant \( FR \): a flat line at \( +FR \) from 0 to \( t_1 \).

angular impulse \( = \tau\Delta t = FR\,t_1 \)

work \( = \tau\Delta\theta = FR\,\theta_1 \)

\( L \) increases, by exactly \( FRt_1 \)

There is a nonzero outside torque in the direction of the spin, so angular momentum flows into the system.
CRepresentations. A \( 0.300\,\mathrm{kg} \) block hangs from a light string wrapped around a uniform disk (\( R = 0.200\,\mathrm{m} \)) on a frictionless axle. Released from rest, it falls \( 0.600\,\mathrm{m} \). Make the energy bar charts, derive \( \omega \), and judge the claim "the disk's \( L \) increases, so angular momentum is conserved."show the answer
Take \( U_g = 0 \) at the bottom. At release: \( U_g = mgy = (0.300)(9.8)(0.600) = 1.764\,\mathrm{J} \), both kinetic energies zero. Halfway: \( U_g = 0.882\,\mathrm{J} \) and \( K_{\text{trans}} + K_{\text{rot}} = 0.882\,\mathrm{J} \), with the heavy disk taking most of it.

\( mgy = \tfrac12 m(R\omega)^2 + \tfrac12 I\omega^2 \Rightarrow \omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{2mgy}{mR^2 + I}} \)

The claim is wrong

For the disk alone, the string's torque is outside, so \( L \) is not conserved. For disk + block, gravity on the block makes an outside torque \( mgR \) about the axle, so \( L \) still grows. Growing \( L \) means it is not conserved.

Quick check · 1 / 17

Question

Don't lose these points

The Unit 6 mistakes that cost the most.

  • 1
    Forgetting the spin energy. A rolling object has \( \tfrac12 Mv^2 \) and \( \tfrac12 I\omega^2 \). Leaving one out gives the wrong speed.
  • 2
    Degrees in \( W = \tau\Delta\theta \) or \( v = r\omega \). Convert to radians first.
  • 3
    Assuming \( L \) is always conserved. Check for an outside torque on the system you picked.
  • 4
    Assuming \( K \) is conserved when \( L \) is. Skaters gain \( K \); sticky collisions lose it.
  • 5
    Mixing up \( L = I\omega \) and \( L = rmv\sin\theta \). Spinning object vs. object moving past a point.
  • 6
    Treating an ellipse like a circle. In an ellipse, \( K \) and \( U_g \) change; only \( E \) and \( L \) stay put.
  • 7
    Positive \( U_g \), or altitude for \( r \). \( U_g \) is negative and \( r \) is measured from the center.
  • 8
    "Friction always wastes energy." Not in rolling without slipping. And \( v = r\omega \) fails once it slips.

Free-response gold

Never stop at "by conservation of energy." Say what the law means for this system, what is different between the cases, and finish with your claim.

add K_rotradiansoutside torque?L ✓ ≠ K ✓which L formula?ellipse ≠ circleU_g < 0static = no loss

Fiveable's practice data shows orbits (6.6) and angular momentum (6.3) are the most-missed topics in this unit. Spend extra time there.

That's the unit

You can follow energy and momentum around a spin now.

Spinning stores \( \tfrac12 I\omega^2 \). Torques move energy with \( \tau\Delta\theta \) and momentum with \( \tau\Delta t \). With no outside twist, \( L \) stays put. Rolling adds \( v = r\omega \). And satellites ride on constant \( E \) and \( L \).
